To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the transsaccadically coded position of a translating target is better detected than the position of a stationary target, but not the position of a saccade target, and that this is specific to translating objects.
the transsaccadically represented position of a translating target object is better detected than that of a stationary target, but the reverse is true for the position of a stationary flanker object.

(1) transsaccadic position shifts of moving objects are detected better than stationary objects, and that this effect is specific to position shifts of translating objects; (2) the effect is not due to a bias in attention towards moving objects; (3) the effect is also not due to the fact that the position of a moving object is more relevant for behavior than a stationary object.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how the brain represents visual objects in the presence of eye movements.
the transsaccadically coded position of objects in a scene and the way it is affected by their motion.
the question of how the visual system deals with the fact that the visual world is constantly changing during saccadic eye movements.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a transsaccadic memory of the location of a translating object, but not a transsaccadically remembered orientation of a rotating object.
there is no evidence of a transsaccadic memory for the position of stationary objects.
transsaccadic object representation is a function of the object's motion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the transsaccadically coded representation of translating objects is qualitatively different from the representation of stationary objects.
saccades do not erase information from the visual world but rather that the information is not available for report.
the representation of the spatial position of a translating target in the saccade program and in the post-saccadic percept is qualitatively different from that of a stationary target.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the saccadic system is able to detect intrasacadic displacements and rotations of moving objects and that the representation of these displacements is superior to the representation of stationary objects.
saccades are not a mere means of shifting gaze but also a means for transsaccadic information processing.
the transsaccadically coded representation of moving objects is more detailed than that of stationary objects.
